The Migne text prints inline variant readings ([Al.], [Ver. ms.]), footnote numerals and OCR slips; the variants and numerals are not translated, and the slips are read as corrected (sc = se, (??)exterae = dexterae, cum = eum, haribus = naribus, cremi = eremi, daemon a = daemonia). Variants of some weight: 'of monks' for 'monk'; 'further, and on earth' for 'further in'; 'led' (deducebatur) for 'drawn away'; 'went back' (regrediebatur) for 'goes further on'.

nodes.text: 7. The ages of Paul and Antony. — But to return to the point from which I digressed: when the blessed Paul had already been living a heavenly life on earth for a hundred and thirteen years, and Antony, at ninety, was staying in another solitude (as he himself used to assert), this thought came into his mind, that no monk more perfect than himself had settled in the desert. But as he rested at night it was revealed to him that there was another, further in, much better than himself, whom he ought to set out to visit. At once, as the light broke, the venerable old man, supporting his weak limbs with a staff to guide him, began to want to go he knew not where. And already midday was blazing, with the sun scorching from above, and yet he was not drawn away from the journey he had begun, saying: “I trust in my God that he will in time show me the fellow servant whom he promised me.” No more than this [had he said, when] he sees a man mixed with a horse, to whom the poets' fancy gave the name Hippocentaur. At this sight he arms his forehead by marking it with the saving sign, and says: “Hey, you, in what part does the servant of God live here?” But it, grinding out some barbarous sound, and breaking its words rather than speaking them, sought through jaws bristling with hair to address him gently. And by stretching out its right hand it points out the road he wanted, and so, crossing the open plains in swift flight, it vanished from the eyes of the astonished man. But whether the devil feigned this to frighten him, or whether the desert, fertile as it is in monstrous animals, gives birth to this beast too, we hold uncertain.

8. Fauns and Satyrs; a Satyr brought alive to Alexandria. — So Antony, astonished, and turning over in his mind what he had seen, goes further on. Before long, in a rocky valley, he sees a little man, not large, with hooked nostrils, his forehead rough with horns, the lower part of whose body ended in goats' feet. At this spectacle Antony, like a good warrior, seized the shield of faith and the breastplate of hope; nonetheless the creature I have mentioned offered him fruit of the palm as provisions for the journey, as if hostages of peace. Realising this, Antony checked his step, and, asking who he was, received this answer from him: “I am a mortal, one of the dwellers in the desert, whom the heathen world, deluded by manifold error, worships, calling them Fauns and Satyrs and Incubi. I am acting as envoy of my flock. We ask you to pray for us to our common Lord, who, we have learned, came once for the salvation of the world; and his sound has gone out into all the earth.” As he spoke thus, the aged traveller bathed his face with abundant tears, which the greatness of his joy had poured out as tokens of his heart. For he rejoiced at the glory of Christ and at the downfall of Satan; and at the same time, marvelling that he could understand its speech, and striking the ground with his staff, he said: “Woe to you, Alexandria, who worship monsters in place of God! Woe to you, harlot city, into which the demons of the whole world have flowed together! What will you say now? Beasts speak of Christ, and you worship monsters in place of God.” He had not yet finished his words when the frisking animal fled away as if in winged flight. Lest this stir any scruple of disbelief in anyone, it is vouched for under the emperor Constantius, with the whole world as witness. For a man of this kind was brought alive to Alexandria and provided a great spectacle for the people; and afterwards the lifeless corpse, with salt poured into it so that it should not decay in the summer heat, was carried to Antioch to be seen by the emperor.
